sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each heading name what its section holds?** No, in two places.
   - **"Bicycles and luggage"** (heading at about x 96–386, y 470–505): the paragraph under it covers only bicycles. Someone with a suitcase, a pram or a dog reads the heading, expects an answer, and finds none. They either think they missed it or assume there's no rule.
   - **"Good to know"** (card heading at about x 849–1090, y 175–215): this could sit on any page. It doesn't say what the box holds, which is where the printed timetables are and where changes are posted.
   - **Why:** WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6 (headings describe the topic of their section).
   - **Fix:** either add a luggage sentence (what's allowed, where it goes) or rename the heading "Bicycles". Rename the card heading after what it holds, e.g. "Timetables and changes".
   - Defect (convention, WCAG 2.4.6). Weight: major for "luggage", because it promises an answer passengers act on and doesn't give it. Minor for "Good to know".
2. **Within one screen, does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** No.
   - **Where:** the aside heading "Good to know" (about 36 px, y 175–215) looks clearly larger than the two main section headings "When the boats run" and "Bicycles and luggage" (about 28 px). The aside body text (about 20 px, line height about 30) also looks larger than the main body text (about 18 px, line height about 27).
   - **What the viewer gets:** the side box looks more important than the main content, so after the H1 the eye jumps right to the card instead of reading down the guide. The page also reads as two designs side by side.
   - **Why:** Gerstner, *Designing Programmes* (elements of one kind share one style); Nielsen heuristic 4, Consistency and standards.
   - **Fix:** give the card heading and body the same sizes as the main section headings and body, or make them one step smaller as an aside. Let the border and the button set the card apart, not size.
   - Convention. Weight: minor in this section. The hierarchy critic will likely weigh the pull on the eye.
3. **Vague times in the main section.** The checklist has no line for this; it comes from the copy rules.
   - **Where:** "When the boats run" body (y 365–440) says "between early morning and late evening", "one boat each hour" in winter, and "the last crossing leaves before dusk".
   - **What the viewer gets:** these are the facts a passenger acts on, and none of them is a time. "Before dusk" moves through the season. "In winter" gives no dates. A reader can't tell whether a 6:30 or a 21:00 crossing exists, so a passenger can arrive after the last boat. The section titled "When the boats run" doesn't say when.
   - **Fix:** give the first and last departure times, the winter date range, and the actual last winter crossing (or "last boat 16:20 Nov–Feb"). Otherwise say plainly that times are on the timetable and link to it inline.
   - Defect. Weight: major, since this is the main job of the page.

**What's working.**
- **One clear purpose.** The H1 and subtitle ("A short guide for passengers on the north landing to market quay route") tell a stranger exactly what this is and who it's for, in one read.
- **One sober mood.** One sans family, near-black text, one blue for the single action, and plain hairline borders suit a public-service ferry notice. Nothing is decorative, and nothing fights.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (each kind of element looks the same; headings name their section)

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?"** No. The levels don't line up across the two columns.
   - **Where:** "Good to know", the side card's heading at about (849,178)–(1090,212), looks about 36 px bold. The main section headings, "When the boats run" (96,318) and "Bicycles and luggage" (96,473), look about 28 px bold.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The aside is ranked above the page's own content, so after the H1 the eye jumps right to the card and its blue button, then comes back to the timetable facts on the left. On a guide meant to be read top to bottom, the card's level-two heading outranks the guide's level-two headings.
   - **Why:** Each level should be obvious at a glance and mean the same thing wherever it appears (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*; Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8). The card heading is one size larger than the section headings, which reads as an accident rather than a deliberate rank.
   - **Fix:** Set the card heading at or below the section-heading size, at the same level or one step down.
   - **Type:** Defect. **Weight:** Major. It changes the reading order of the page.
2. **The same line, on near-matching body sizes.** No.
   - **Where:** The card's paragraph ("Printed timetables are kept…", 849,235–380) looks about 20 px. The main body paragraphs (96,365–595) look about 18 px. Both are regular weight, same typeface, and both are plain body text.
   - **What the viewer sees:** Seen side by side, the two blocks almost match but don't. The card text looks slightly louder than the main copy for no reason, which adds to the pull toward the aside.
   - **Why:** "Sizes come from a scale" (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1). Sizes this close show they were picked one at a time. All told the page uses about 7 sizes (~64, 36, 28, 24, 20, 18, 16), where 4 would carry it.
   - **Fix:** Use one body size in both columns. If the card needs to look different, do it with colour or its container, not 2 px more.
   - **Type:** Convention. **Weight:** Minor.

**What's working.**
- The H1 "Crossing the river" (~64 px bold) is far larger than everything else, so the eye has an obvious place to start.
- Every heading differs from its text in weight as well as size. The subtitle drops to a grey regular face, so it reads as a step below the H1 even though its size is close to the H2s.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each text level distinct, no near sizes)

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid?** The answer is no. The header sets the container: the logo starts at x≈96 and the nav ends at x≈1184. The main column follows the left edge at x=96. The "Good to know" card (x≈820–1150) stops about 34 px short of the nav's right edge. That leaves a right margin of ≈130 px against 96 px on the left, so the body looks pushed slightly left of the header, as if the card was sized by eye instead of placed on the container's columns. Müller-Brockmann (*Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid") says every block should take its edges from the same columns and margins. Fix: run the card's right edge to the container edge at x≈1184, or narrow the header to match, so the header and body share one right edge. This is a convention break. **Weight: minor.** The page still reads fine, but the layout looks less finished.
2. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge it shares, or clearly off it, with no near-misses?** The answer is no. The card's top border (y≈147) sits about 10 px below the cap height of "Crossing the river" (y≈137). "Good to know" then lands about halfway between the H1 and the subtitle. The two columns look meant to start together but miss, which Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance") says makes a placement read as an error rather than a choice. Fix: either align the card's top edge with the H1's cap height, or drop the card clearly, for example to line up with "When the boats run" at y≈318. This is a convention break, and the source is only partly confirmed. **Weight: minor.**
3. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?** The answer is no. Card body lines (y≈246–367) step about 30 px apart and main body lines step about 27 px. The card's body type is also larger than the main body type. Side by side, the two columns drift out of line, and the sidebar looks set in a different system. Fix: put the card text on the main column's size and line height, or on a multiple of it, so the baselines line up. This is taste: in a boxed sidebar, baseline alignment matters less than it does for open parallel columns. **Weight: minor.**

**What's working.**
- Grouping by space is clear. Each H2 sits about 20 px above its paragraph and about 35 px below the previous one, so "When the boats run" and "Bicycles and luggage" read as two separate units without rules or boxes.
- The empty space is gathered. The open band below y≈600 and the area under the card are large, quiet areas that give the dense left column room to breathe. It isn't spread thinly between every element.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (one grid; exact alignment or clearly off; baselines across columns).

The walk and deep read are done: one minor finding, with the report below.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** No, in the "Good to know" card (paragraph at about x 849–1120, y 233–380). The card's body text looks about 20 px. That is larger than the main column's body at about 17 px, and it sits in a column about 270 px wide. So the lines run only about 25–27 characters ("Printed timetables are kept", "lists any changes for the"), and the line breaks fall on almost every phrase. The reader turns back five times to read one sentence, and the note reads choppier than the main text, even though it is shorter. Bringhurst (*The Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.1.2) gives 45–75 characters for a single column and 40–50 for text set in several columns. The card is well under both. Fix: set the card text at body size or a step below so it ranks as a side note, which gives about 32 or more characters a line, or widen the card. **Convention. Weight: minor.** The paragraph is one sentence, so the cost is choppiness, not lost place. The card body being larger than the main body is also a hierarchy question for that critic.

**What's working.**
- The main column's measure and spacing are right. The body paragraphs run about 65–68 characters ("The ferry leaves every forty minutes between early morning and late") with line spacing of about 1.6. The text is a single sans family in regular and bold, and it reads easily with no effort.
- The copy is in short chunks. Two small headings ("When the boats run", "Bicycles and luggage") each have a 3-line paragraph, so a passenger scanning for one answer finds it at once. The subhead "Crossing the river" is spaced slightly tighter than the text and the gaps between its letters look even at that size.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters)

The image is 1280×800, which is about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. I didn't need the crop script.

**First read.** The eye lands on "Crossing the river", then moves to the "Good to know" card and its blue button. It reads as a plain, calm information page for ferry passengers.

**Walk: Color**
- Small palette: yes. Near-black text, one mid-gray for the subtitle, pale gray rules and card border, and one blue for the button.
- Saturated colour kept to a small share of the area: yes. The blue button is the only saturated area.
- Clear range of light and dark, structure shows in grayscale: yes.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. The page has no warm colour. The one cool blue comes forward through saturation and darkness alone, and that suits the piece.
- Matching colours look the same: yes.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colour used for its usual meaning: yes. Blue is used for an action, which is what users expect.
- Meaning not carried by colour alone: yes. The button reads as a button from its shape and label.
- Dark theme uses dark gray: yes. The page is light, so this doesn't apply.

Every line was answered yes, so no entries needed a deep read.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
1. **One accent, used once.** The blue appears only on "See the timetable" (about 849–1025 × 402–446 px). It is the only saturated colour on a page that is otherwise neutral, so the eye finds the main action without any other emphasis. Keep that blue for actions only.
2. **Gray steps show the hierarchy.** Headings and body text are near-black, the subtitle (96–690 × 215–280 px) is a clearly lighter gray, and the header rule and card border are paler still. Each level of importance has its own lightness, so the structure would still read in grayscale.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes.

sections.report:
Interface walk (working notes):

The image is 1280×800, so one screen and no crops were needed. The page is a ferry company's passenger guide. It has a header with a wordmark and three nav links, plus one button in a side card.

- One primary action: yes. The blue "See the timetable" button is the only filled control.
- Controls look like what they do: yes. The button is a filled rectangle, and the nav links sit in a conventional header row.
- Non-text contrast: yes. The button's fill against white is strong. The card border is pale, but it isn't a control.
- Hover, pressed and disabled states shown: yes, because none are shown.
- Focus indicator: unsure, since a still can't show it.
- Focus not obscured: unsure. I can't tell whether the header is sticky.
- Main content uncovered: yes.
- Target size: yes. The button looks about 176×44. The nav link text looks about 20 px tall, with roughly 30 px gaps, so the spacing exception holds.
- Phone thumb zone: yes (not applicable).
- Where the user is: yes. This reads as the home page, and the wordmark stands for home. No nav item needs to be marked current.
- Way out, valid inputs, destructive actions: yes (not applicable).
- Recognition rather than recall: yes.
- Progressive disclosure: yes.
- Form lines (labels, single column, required markers, errors, error fixes): yes (not applicable).
- Empty state: yes (not applicable).
- Help near the step: yes.
- Shortcuts: yes. The nav jumps straight to Timetable, Fares and Landings.
- Anticipation: yes. The timetable button sits next to the schedule talk.
- Conventions: yes.
- Audience's own words: yes.
- Link purpose: yes.
- Sensory instructions: yes.
- Conceptual model: yes.
- Consistency across screens: yes (only one screen).
- Reflow: yes.
- Honest choices: yes.

**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a header nav with three links and one call-to-action button.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One clear action.** "See the timetable" at about (849–1025, 402–446) is the only filled control on the page. It sits right under the card text about printed timetables and noticeboard changes, so the step that answers "when does the next boat leave?" is where the reader already is. Its label names what you'll get, not a vague "Learn more."
- **The nav fits the job.** The header links at about (935–1184, 41) are Timetable, Fares and Landings. These are the three things a ferry passenger comes to check, in plain words. They sit in the usual top-right spot next to the wordmark, so nobody has to hunt for them.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Focus on the nav links and the button.** Check in a browser that the focus ring is at least 2 px with 3:1 contrast, especially on the blue button, where a default blue ring could disappear.
- **Whether the header is sticky.** If it is, check that it doesn't cover a focused element when someone tabs or scrolls.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 0 no, 2 unsure (focus indicator on the nav links and button; whether the header is sticky and could cover a focused control)
